questions.question: Under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, for how long can a suspect be detained without a magistrate's approval?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**24 hours**__.

**__Key Points__**

• Under the **Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023**, specifically **Section 58**, a person arrested without a warrant cannot be detained by a police officer for more than **24 hours**.

• This **24-hour** limit is calculated excluding the **time necessary for the journey** from the place of arrest to the **Magistrate’s Court**.

• The primary objective of this provision is to prevent **arbitrary detention** and ensure that the **Judiciary** has immediate oversight over the **Executive’s** power to arrest.

• This legal requirement is a statutory reflection of the fundamental right guaranteed under **Article 22(2)** of the Constitution of India</strong

questions.question:
Fill in the blank:
The PM Vishwakarma scheme provides financial assistance and skill training to ________
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Artisans and craftsmen**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **PM Vishwakarma Scheme** is a Central Sector Scheme designed to provide end-to-end support to **artisans and craftsmen** who work with their hands and tools.

• The primary objective is to strengthen and nurture the **Guru-Shishya parampara** (traditional family-based practice) of passing on traditional skills by **Vishwakarmas**.

• The scheme covers **18 traditional trades**, including carpenters, boat makers, blacksmiths, hammer and tool kit makers, locksmiths, goldsmiths, potters, sculptors, cobblers, masons, basket/mat/broom makers, doll and toy makers, barbers, garland makers, washermen, tailors, and fishing net makers.

• Benefits include **recognition** through a PM Vishwakarma certificate and ID card, **skill upgradation** (basic and advanced training), a **toolkit incentive** of 15,000 rupees, and **collateral-free credit support**.

• While **Farmers** are supported by schemes like **PM-KISAN**, and **Street vendors** are covered under **PM SVANidhi**, the PM Vishwakarma scheme specifically targets the traditional artisan community.

**Additional Information__**

• The scheme was officially launched by the Prime Minister on **September 17, 2023**, on the occasion of **Vishwakarma Jayanti**.

• It has a total financial outlay of **13,000 crore rupees** for a period of five years (FY 2023-24 to FY 2027-28).

• Artisans can avail credit support up to **3 lakh rupees** in two tranches (1 lakh and 2 lakh) at a highly concessional interest rate of **5%**.

• The scheme is implemented by the **Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME)**, the **Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship**, and the **Department of Financial Services**.
</ul

questions.question: Under which of the following circumstances the Parliament of India can legislate on the matters listed in the State List?

options.text: If there is a need to regulate local government elections
If there is a need to impose state-level taxes
If there is a need to appoint new state ministers
If there is a need to implement an international treaty

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**If there is a need to implement an international treaty**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Article 253** of the **Constitution of India** explicitly empowers the **Parliament** to make any law for the whole or any part of the territory of **India** for implementing any **treaty**, **agreement**, or **convention** with any other country or countries, or any decision made at any international conference, association, or other body. This allows the **Union Government** to legislate on matters even if they are listed in the **State List**. *Hence, statement 4 is correct.*

• The regulation of **local government elections** is a subject primarily under the jurisdiction of the **State Legislature**. According to **Entry 5** of the **State List** and **Articles 243K** and **243ZA**, the power to conduct and regulate these elections is vested in the **State Election Commission**. **Parliament** does not have the general authority to legislate on this under normal circumstances. *Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.*

• The power to impose **state-level taxes**, such as **land revenue**, **taxes on agricultural income**, or **taxes on mineral rights**, is an exclusive legislative power of the **State** as per the **Seventh Schedule**. **Parliament** cannot generally legislate on these taxes unless a **National Emergency** is in place or other specific constitutional exceptions apply. *Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.*

• The **appointment of state ministers** is an executive function governed by **Article 164** of the **Constitution**. The **Governor** appoints the **Chief Minister** and other ministers on the advice of the **Chief Minister**. This is a matter of state executive process and does not fall under the legislative domain of the **Parliament**. *Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.*

**Additional Information__**
__

• The **Seventh Schedule** (Article 246) of the **Indian Constitution** divides legislative powers into three lists: the **Union List** (List I), the **State List** (List II), and the **Concurrent List** (List III). While the **State List** is usually the exclusive domain of **States**, the **Constitution** provides specific scenarios where **Parliament** can intervene.

• **Article 249**: If the **Rajya Sabha** passes a resolution supported by not less than **two-thirds** of the members present and voting that it is necessary or expedient in the **national interest**, **Parliament** can make laws with respect to any matter in the **State List**. Such a law remains in force for **one year**.

• **Article 250**: During the operation of a **Proclamation of Emergency**, **Parliament** acquires the power to legislate on any matter enumerated in the **State List** for the whole or any part of **India**. These laws cease to have effect **six months** after the emergency ends.

• **Article 252**: If the **Legislatures** of **two or more states** pass resolutions requesting **Parliament** to enact a law on a state subject, **Parliament** can pass such an act. This act applies only to the requesting states and any other state that adopts it later by a resolution.

• **Article 248**: This article confers **residuary powers** of legislation upon the **Parliament**, meaning any matter not mentioned in any of the three lists falls under the exclusive jurisdiction of the **Union**.

**Important Points__**

• **Article 356**: When **President's Rule** is imposed in a state due to the failure of constitutional machinery, the **Parliament** is authorized to exercise the legislative powers of that **State Legislature**.

• The **Environment Protection Act, 1986** and the **Wild Life (Protection) Act, 1972** are prominent examples of laws enacted by the **Parliament** under **Article 253** to fulfill **international obligations** arising from the **Stockholm Conference** of **1972**.

• The **Sarkaria Commission** (established in **1983**) and the **Punchhi Commission** (established in **2007**) both reviewed **Centre-State relations** and emphasized that while the **federal structure** is essential, the **Union's** power to implement **international treaties** is vital for **national integrity** and **foreign policy**.

• Under **Article 253**, the **Parliament** can even legislate on subjects like **agriculture** or **public health** (which are in the **State List**) if it is necessary to comply with **international agreements** like those of the **World Trade Organization (WTO)**.
</ul

questions.question: Where was the first Cricket World Cup held in 1975?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**England**__.

**__Key Points__**

__

• The **first-ever Cricket World Cup** was officially known as the **Prudential Cup** and was held in **England** in **June 1975**. **England** was the only nation at that time that had the resources and infrastructure to host such a massive international event.

• The tournament was organized by the **International Cricket Conference** (now known as the **International Cricket Council** or **ICC**). It featured **eight teams**: **Australia**, **England**, **India**, **New Zealand**, **Pakistan**, the **West Indies**, **Sri Lanka**, and **East Africa**.

• The matches in the **1975** edition were played in a **60-over** format per side, which is different from the current **50-over** standard. Players wore **traditional white clothing** and used **red cricket balls**.

• The **West Indies** emerged as the inaugural champions by defeating **Australia** in the final by **17 runs**. The final was held at the iconic **Lord’s Cricket Ground** in **London** on **June 21, 1975**.

• Regarding the other options: **India** did not host the World Cup until **1987**; **Australia** first co-hosted the event in **1992**; and the **West Indies** hosted their first World Cup much later in **2007**. Hence, **England** is the correct location for the **1975** event.

**Additional Information__**

__

• **West Indies Dominance**: The **West Indies** team, captained by **Clive Lloyd**, was a powerhouse in early world cricket. They won the first two editions of the World Cup in **1975** and **1979**, both held in **England**. **Clive Lloyd** scored a brilliant **102 runs** in the **1975 final** to secure the victory.

• **Host Rotation**: **England** hosted the first three World Cups (**1975**, **1979**, and **1983**). It was only in **1987** that the tournament moved out of **England** to the **Indian subcontinent** (hosted by **India** and **Pakistan**).

• **Evolution of Format**: The **1987 World Cup** saw the reduction of overs from **60** to **50** per innings to accommodate the shorter daylight hours in the **Asian subcontinent** compared to the **English summer**.

• **Historical Significance**: The **1975 World Cup** marked the global expansion of **One Day International (ODI)** cricket, which had only begun in **1971**. It paved the way for cricket to become a major commercial and televised sport worldwide.

• **East Africa Team**: A unique feature of the **1975** tournament was the participation of the **East Africa** team, which represented players from **Kenya**, **Uganda**, **Tanzania**, and **Zambia**.

**Important Points__**

• **First Match**: The opening match of the **1975 World Cup** was played between **England** and **India** at **Lord’s**. It is famously remembered for **Sunil Gavaskar** scoring an unbeaten **36 runs** off **174 balls**, a very slow innings for an **ODI**.

• **Sponsorship**: The tournament was sponsored by the **Prudential Assurance Company**, which provided a total prize fund of **£9,000**, with the winners receiving **£4,000**.

• **Venue Details**: Matches were spread across several historic venues in **England**, including **The Oval** (London), **Old Trafford** (Manchester), **Trent Bridge** (Nottingham), **Headingley** (Leeds), and **Edgbaston** (Birmingham).

• **Recent Edition**: The most recent **ICC Men’s Cricket World Cup** was held in **2023** in **India**, where **Australia** defeated **India** in the final to claim their **sixth title**.

questions.question: BIMSTEC stands for?

options.text: Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation
Bangladesh India Maritime Security and Trade Economic Council
Bhutan India Myanmar South Asia Trade Economic Cooperation
Bay of Bengal International Maritime and Security Treaty

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **BIMSTEC** stands for the **Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation**. It is a regional multilateral organization comprising seven Member States in the littoral and adjacent areas of the **Bay of Bengal**. Hence, the statement in option 1 is correct.

• The organization was established on **6 June 1997** through the signing of the **Bangkok Declaration**. It was initially formed with four member states and was known as **BIST-EC** (**Bangladesh, India, Sri Lanka, and Thailand Economic Cooperation**).

• The **Permanent Secretariat** of **BIMSTEC** is located in **Dhaka, Bangladesh**. It was inaugurated in **2014** to provide institutionalized support for the activities of the group and to coordinate the implementation of various projects.

• The membership of the organization currently includes five countries from **South Asia** (**Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Nepal, and Sri Lanka**) and two countries from **Southeast Asia** (**Myanmar and Thailand**).

• The other options provided, such as **Bangladesh India Maritime Security and Trade Economic Council**, **Bhutan India Myanmar South Asia Trade Economic Cooperation**, and **Bay of Bengal International Maritime and Security Treaty**, are incorrect expansions and do not represent any official international body. Hence, statements 2, 3, and 4 are incorrect.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Evolution of Membership**: After its inception in **1997**, the group expanded to include **Myanmar** on **22 December 1997**, changing the name to **BIMST-EC**. In **February 2004**, **Nepal** and **Bhutan** became full members, leading to the current name.

• **Economic Significance**: The **BIMSTEC** region is home to approximately **1.5 billion people**, which constitutes around **22%** of the total global population. The member states have a combined **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** of over **3.5 trillion USD**.

• **Institutional Structure**: The **Chairmanship** of **BIMSTEC** rotates among the member states in alphabetical order. **Thailand** took over the chairmanship from **Sri Lanka** for the **2022-2023** period.

• **Sectors of Cooperation**: Cooperation within **BIMSTEC** was initially divided into **14 sectors**, including **Trade, Technology, Energy, Transport, Tourism, and Fisheries**. Recently, these were reorganized into **7 pillars**, with each member state leading one pillar. **India** is the lead country for the **Security** pillar.

**Important Points__**

• **BIMSTEC Charter**: A significant milestone was achieved during the **Fifth BIMSTEC Summit** held in **Colombo, Sri Lanka**, on **30 March 2022**, where the **BIMSTEC Charter** was signed. This charter provides the organization with a formal legal personality.

• **Connectivity Projects**: The organization emphasizes regional integration through projects like the **BIMSTEC Master Plan for Transport Connectivity**. Key initiatives include the **Kaladan Multi-modal Transit Transport Project** and the **Asian Highway Network**, aimed at linking **India** with **Southeast Asia**.

• **Strategic Importance for India**: For **India**, **BIMSTEC** serves as a crucial platform to fulfill its **Neighborhood First** and **Act East** policies. It provides a functional alternative to **SAARC**, which has been stagnant due to regional tensions.

• **Free Trade Agreement (FTA)**: The member nations signed the **BIMSTEC Free Trade Area Framework Agreement** in **2004** to stimulate trade and investment. Negotiations are ongoing to finalize the **BIMSTEC FTA** to further reduce tariffs and non-tariff barriers.
</ul

questions.question: What is the purpose of the Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO) mission?

options.text: To study the cosmic microwave background radiation
To provide insights into the sun
To monitor the Earth's magnetic field

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To provide insights into the sun**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Solar and Heliospheric Observatory (SOHO)** is a joint international project between the **European Space Agency (ESA)** and **NASA**.

• Launched on **December 2, 1995**, its primary objective is to investigate the **Sun** from its deep core to the outer **corona** and the **solar wind**.

• The observatory is stationed at the **First Lagrangian Point (L1)**, which is a gravitationally stable point located about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth toward the Sun. This position allows SOHO to maintain a **constant, uninterrupted view** of the Sun.

• The mission aims to solve three fundamental questions in solar physics: the **internal structure** of the Sun, the mechanism behind the **heating of the solar corona**, and where the **solar wind** is produced and how it is accelerated.

• SOHO provides real-time data that is essential for **space weather forecasting**, helping to predict solar storms that can affect satellites, telecommunications, and power grids on Earth.

**Additional Information__**

• SOHO is the most successful **comet hunter** in history, having discovered over **4,000 comets** (mostly 'sungrazing' comets) during its mission.

• The spacecraft is equipped with **12 scientific instruments**, including the **LASCO (Large Angle and Spectrometric Coronagraph)**, which blocks the Sun's direct light to observe the much fainter corona.

• While originally designed for a **two-year mission**, SOHO has been operational for nearly **three decades**, allowing scientists to observe more than two full **11-year solar cycles**.

• The study of the **cosmic microwave background (CMB)** radiation mentioned in other options is the domain of missions like **COBE**, **WMAP**, and **Planck**, not SOHO.
</ul

questions.question: How have human-induced disturbances impacted terrestrial ecosystems?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Through changes in land use**__

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Human-induced disturbances** have significantly impacted **terrestrial ecosystems** primarily through **land use changes**, which include activities such as **deforestation**, **urbanization**, and the conversion of natural landscapes into **agricultural land**.

• **Deforestation** for timber or farming leads to the immediate loss of **habitats**, reduction in **biodiversity**, and disruption of the **carbon cycle**.

• **Urbanization** results in **habitat fragmentation**, where large, continuous ecosystems are broken into smaller, isolated patches, making it difficult for species to survive and migrate.

• **Agricultural expansion** often involves the use of **monocultures**, which reduces the resilience of the ecosystem and alters **soil health** and **nutrient cycling**.

• While **rising ocean temperatures** (Option 3) are a result of human activity, they primarily impact **marine ecosystems** rather than being a direct terrestrial disturbance.

• **Atmospheric CO2 concentrations** (Option 4) have actually **increased** due to human activities like burning **fossil fuels**, rather than decreased.

**Additional Information__**

• According to the **Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)**, approximately 75% of the Earth's ice-free land surface has been significantly altered by **human actions**.

• **Anthropogenic disturbances** also include the introduction of **invasive species**, **pollution** (pesticides and heavy metals), and **overexploitation** of natural resources.

• **Land degradation** caused by human activity affects the livelihoods of billions of people and contributes to **climate change** by releasing stored carbon from vegetation and soils.

• The **United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 15** specifically aims to protect, restore, and promote the sustainable use of **terrestrial ecosystems** and halt **biodiversity loss**.
</ul

questions.question: What is the primary function of the xylem tissue in plants?

options.text: To transport products of photosynthesis from leaves to other parts of the plant
To transport water and minerals obtained from the soil
To provide energy to the plant

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To transport water and minerals obtained from the soil**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Xylem** is a specialized type of **vascular tissue** in plants primarily responsible for the **upward conduction** of **water** and **dissolved minerals** from the roots to the leaves and stems.
 
• The transport in xylem is **unidirectional**, meaning it only moves from the soil/roots upwards to the aerial parts of the plant.
 
• It consists of four main components: **Tracheids**, **Vessels** (tracheary elements), **Xylem Parenchyma**, and **Xylem Fibers**.
 
• The transport of **photosynthetic products** (like sucrose) is the primary function of **Phloem**, not xylem.
 
• **Glucose synthesis** occurs in the **chloroplasts** of leaf cells through the process of **photosynthesis**, while energy is provided through **cellular respiration** in the mitochondria.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Xylem also provides **mechanical strength** and structural support to the plant body due to the presence of **lignified** cell walls.
 
• Except for **xylem parenchyma**, all other xylem elements (tracheids, vessels, and fibers) are **dead cells** at maturity.
 
• The movement of water through the xylem is driven by physical forces such as **transpiration pull** (suction created by evaporation from leaves) and **root pressure**.
 
• In **Angiosperms**, vessels are the main water-conducting elements, whereas in **Gymnosperms**, tracheids are the primary conductors as they lack true vessels.

questions.question: What happens to the pupil in low light conditions?

options.text: It contracts to prevent excess light from entering
It expands to allow more light to enter

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**It expands to allow more light to enter**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**
__

• The **pupil** is the dark circular opening in the center of the **iris** that regulates the amount of light entering the eye.

• In **low light conditions** or darkness, the pupil **dilates** (expands). This is a physiological response to allow the maximum possible amount of light to reach the **retina**, helping the person see better in the dark.

• This expansion is controlled by the **radial muscles** of the iris, which contract to pull the pupil open wider.

• In contrast, in **bright light**, the pupil **constricts** (shrinks) to prevent too much light from entering, which could damage the sensitive cells of the retina. This is controlled by the **circular muscles** of the iris.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• The **iris** is the colored part of the eye that acts like a shutter in a camera, adjusting the size of the pupil.

• The adjustment of the pupil size in response to light intensity is known as the **pupillary light reflex**.

• The **retina** contains two main types of photoreceptor cells: **rods**, which are sensitive to low light levels (scotopic vision), and **cones**, which are responsible for color vision and high spatial acuity (photopic vision).

• The **optic nerve** transmits the visual information from the retina to the **brain** for processing.
</ul

questions.question: What is the main objective of a government budget?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**To allocate public funds**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The primary objective of a **Government Budget** is the **Reallocation of Resources**. The government aims to distribute **public funds** into various sectors to balance the goals of **profit maximization** and **social welfare**. This ensures that essential services and **public goods** like **defense**, **roads**, and **healthcare** are funded adequately. ***Hence, option 2 is correct.***

• **Reducing Inequalities in Income and Wealth**: The budget serves as a tool for **redistribution**. By imposing higher **taxes** on the rich and providing **subsidies** or **transfer payments** to the poor, the government strives to achieve **social justice**.

• **Economic Stability**: A budget is designed to prevent **economic fluctuations** such as **inflation** or **deflation**. Through **fiscal policy** measures, the government maintains **price stability** and ensures the economy operates near full capacity.

• **Management of Public Enterprises**: Many **socially important sectors** like **railways**, **electricity**, and **water supply** are managed by the government. The budget provides the necessary **financial framework** for the operation and expansion of these **Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs)**.

• **Economic Growth**: The budget focuses on increasing the **Gross Domestic Product (GDP)** by providing **tax incentives**, **investment grants**, and spending on **infrastructure** to encourage **savings** and **capital formation**.

• The objective to **increase unemployment** is fundamentally opposite to the goals of any government budget, as budgets aim for **full employment** and **poverty alleviation**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• While **decreasing taxes** can be a strategy within a budget to boost **consumption**, it is not the **main objective** because the government requires **revenue** to function. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• While the budget may create a favorable environment for the **private sector**, its core mandate is the management of **public finances** for the **common good** rather than solely promoting private interests. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• In **India**, the budget is constitutionally termed the **Annual Financial Statement** under **Article 112** of the **Constitution of India**. It is a statement of the estimated **receipts** and **expenditure** of the **Government of India** for a specific **financial year**.

• The **Financial Year** in **India** begins on **1st April** and ends on **31st March** of the following year.

• A budget is divided into two main parts: the **Revenue Budget** (dealing with **tax revenue**, **interest**, and **salaries**) and the **Capital Budget** (dealing with **assets**, **liabilities**, **loans**, and **infrastructure**).

• **Types of Budgets**:

• **Balanced Budget**: When estimated **government receipts** are equal to estimated **expenditure**.

• **Surplus Budget**: When estimated **receipts** exceed estimated **expenditure**, often used to control **inflation**.

• **Deficit Budget**: When estimated **expenditure** exceeds estimated **receipts**, typically used by **developing countries** to stimulate **economic growth**.

**Important Points__**

• The **Union Budget** is presented by the **Union Finance Minister** in the **Parliament**, specifically in the **Lok Sabha**.

• Historically, **India** had a separate **Railway Budget** and **General Budget**. However, following the **Vivek Debroy Committee** recommendations, the two were merged in **2017**.

• The **Budget Division** of the **Department of Economic Affairs**, under the **Ministry of Finance**, is the nodal body responsible for preparing the budget.

• The **Economic Survey** is usually presented a day before the budget to provide a summary of the **economic performance** of the country in the **past year**.

• **Fiscal Deficit** is a key indicator monitored in the budget, representing the total **borrowings** needed by the government to meet its **expenditure**.
</ul

questions.question: Which feature of Mughal architecture was inspired by Persian styles?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Large domes and iwans (vaulted halls)**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Mughal architecture** is a remarkably symmetrical and decorative amalgam of **Persian**, **Turki**, and **Indian** architectural styles that flourished in the **Indian subcontinent** from the **16th** to the **18th century**.

• The feature of **Large domes** and **iwans** (vaulted halls) was directly inspired by **Persian (Safavid)** and **Central Asian (Timurid)** traditions. An **Iwan** is a rectangular hall or space, usually vaulted, walled on three sides, with one end entirely open; this became a signature element of **Mughal** gateways and mosque facades. ***Hence, statement 2 is correct.***

• **Flat roofs and simple courtyards** are more characteristic of **indigenous Indian** styles or the earlier **Delhi Sultanate** period, rather than being a specific **Persian** innovation introduced by the **Mughals**. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***

• **Stepwells** (known as **Baolis**) and elaborate **pavilions** are traditional **Indian** architectural features found extensively in **Rajasthan** and **Gujarat** long before the **Mughal** era. While **Mughals** built them, they were not **Persian** inspirations. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***

• **Minimal ornamentation** is the opposite of **Mughal** aesthetics, which are world-renowned for **lavish decoration**, including **carvings**, **frescoes**, and **inlay work**. **Persian** influence actually brought more complex decorative patterns to **India**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Humayun’s Tomb**: Built in **1570** in **Delhi**, it was the first major **Mughal** structure to showcase strong **Persian** influence, designed by the **Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas**. It introduced the **double dome** and the **Charbagh** layout to **India**.

• **Charbagh Layout**: This is a **Persian-style** garden layout where a quadrilateral garden is divided by **walkways** or **flowing water** into four smaller parts. This symbolizes the **Islamic** concept of **Paradise**.

• **Pietra Dura**: During the reign of **Shah Jahan** (**1628–1658**), the **Persian** technique of **Pietra Dura** (inlaying semi-precious stones like **lapis lazuli**, **jade**, and **crystal** into **marble**) reached its zenith, most famously seen in the **Taj Mahal**.

• **Double Dome**: This **Persian** architectural technique involves an inner shell to provide a ceiling in proportion with the interior and an outer shell to give the building a **monumental height** and **grandeur** from the outside.

**Important Points__**

• **Evolution of Materials**: Early **Mughal** structures under **Emperor Akbar** primarily used **Red Sandstone** (e.g., **Fatehpur Sikri**, built in **1571**), while later structures under **Shah Jahan** shifted toward **White Marble** to reflect **purity** and **elegance**.

• **Bulbous Domes**: The **onion-shaped** or **bulbous dome**, a distinct **Persian** feature, became more pronounced in later **Mughal** architecture, such as the **Taj Mahal** (completed in **1653**) and the **Bibi Ka Maqbara** in **Aurangabad**.

• **Calligraphy**: **Persian** influence also brought the use of **Arabic** and **Persian calligraphy** as a form of architectural decoration, often featuring **Quranic verses** inscribed on the **iwans** and **arches**.

• **Symmetry**: A core principle of **Persian** design adopted by the **Mughals** was **absolute bilateral symmetry**, where every element on one side of an axis is mirrored on the other, creating a sense of **harmony** and **balance**.

45

questions.question: Which year marked the completion of Rashtrapati Bhavan?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1929**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The construction of the **Rashtrapati Bhavan**, originally known as the **Viceroy's House**, was completed in the year **1929**. The project was a massive undertaking that spanned nearly **17 years** from its inception to its final completion. **Hence, this option is correct.**

• The year **1912** marked the **commencement** of the construction work on **Raisina Hill**. This followed the **1911** announcement by **King George V** during the **Delhi Durbar** that the capital of **British India** would be shifted from **Calcutta** to **Delhi**. Hence, this option is incorrect as it refers to the start, not the completion.

• The year **1921** is significant in the history of **New Delhi** as the **foundation stone** of the **Council House** (now known as the **Old Parliament House** or **Sansad Bhavan**) was laid by the **Duke of Connaught**, but the **Viceroy's House** was still in the middle of its construction phase during this time. Hence, this option is incorrect.

• The year **1935** is historically important for the **Government of India Act 1935**, which introduced significant constitutional reforms. However, the **Rashtrapati Bhavan** had already been completed and occupied by the **Viceroy** for several years by then. Hence, this option is incorrect.

• The primary architect responsible for the design was **Sir Edwin Lutyens**, who worked alongside **Herbert Baker**. Lutyens was tasked with creating a residence that would symbolize the permanence of **British rule** in India, resulting in a structure that covers a floor area of **200,000 square feet**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• The building comprises **four floors** and **340 rooms**, including the **Durbar Hall**, **Ashoka Hall**, and various guest suites. It is surrounded by a massive estate of **330 acres**, which includes the famous **Amrit Udyan** (formerly **Mughal Gardens**).

• The architectural style is a unique blend of **Mughal**, **Hindu**, and **Western Classical** influences. Notable Indian features include **chhatris** (dome-shaped pavilions), **jaalis** (perforated stone screens), and **chajjas** (overhanging eaves).

• The first resident of the building was **Lord Irwin**, the **Viceroy of India**, who moved into the house on **January 23, 1931**. After India gained independence, **C. Rajagopalachari** became the first Indian to reside there as the **Governor-General** in **1948**.

• The construction involved the use of approximately **700 million bricks** and **3 million cubic feet of stone**. The exterior is primarily made of **red and cream sandstone**, which was sourced from **Bharatpur** and **Dholpur**.

• The **Jaipur Column**, which stands in the center of the **Forecourt**, was a gift from the **Maharaja of Jaipur**, **Sawai Madho Singh**, to commemorate the building of the new capital city.

• The **Durbar Hall** is the most significant room within the building, located directly under the main dome. It is used for high-profile state ceremonies, such as the presentation of **Civilian and Military Awards** (like the **Bharat Ratna** and **Padma Awards**) and the **swearing-in** of the **Prime Minister** and the **Council of Ministers**.

questions.question: Who composed the famous Carnatic music work 'Pancharatna Kritis'?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Tyagaraja**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **Tyagaraja** (**1767–1847**) was a legendary composer and a saint of **Carnatic music** who lived in **Thiruvaiyaru**, **Tamil Nadu**. He is the composer of the **Pancharatna Kritis**, which are considered the most significant and masterful of his works. **Hence, the correct answer is Tyagaraja.**

• The **Pancharatna Kritis**, meaning **Five Gems**, are a set of five musical compositions dedicated to **Lord Rama**. They are composed in the **Ghanaraga Panchaka**, which refers to five traditional **heavy ragas**: **Nata**, **Gaula**, **Arabhi**, **Varali**, and **Sri**.

• **Purandara Dasa** (**1484–1564**) is revered as the **Pitamaha** (Grandfather) of **Carnatic music** for codifying the basic lessons and structure of the art form. However, he did not compose the **Pancharatna Kritis**. **Hence, option 2 is incorrect.**

• **Muthuswami Dikshitar** (**1775–1835**) was a contemporary of **Tyagaraja** and a member of the **Trinity of Carnatic Music**. He is famous for his **Sanskrit** compositions and the **Navagraha Kritis**, but not the **Pancharatna Kritis**. **Hence, option 3 is incorrect.**

• **Shyama Shastri** (**1762–1827**) is the oldest member of the **Trinity**. He is renowned for his mastery over **Tala** (rhythm) and his famous **Swarajatis** dedicated to **Goddess Kamakshi**. **Hence, option 4 is incorrect.**

**Additional Information__**
__

• **The Trinity of Carnatic Music**: This refers to the three most influential composers of the **18th** and **19th centuries**—**Tyagaraja**, **Muthuswami Dikshitar**, and **Shyama Shastri**. All three were born in **Tiruvarur** and revolutionized **South Indian classical music**.

• **Tyagaraja Aradhana**: This is a world-famous **annual music festival** held in **Thiruvaiyaru** to honor the **samadhi** (passing) of **Saint Tyagaraja**. During this festival, hundreds of musicians gather to sing the **Pancharatna Kritis** in unison as a tribute.

• **Language of Compositions**: **Tyagaraja** primarily composed in **Telugu**, which was the court language of the **Thanjavur Maratha kingdom** at the time. He also composed several pieces in **Sanskrit**.

• **Musical Contribution of Purandara Dasa**: He is credited with creating the **Sarali Varisai**, **Jantai Varisai**, and **Alankaras**, which are the foundational exercises for every student of **Carnatic music**. He composed in **Kannada**.

• **Muthuswami Dikshitar's Style**: His compositions are known for their **slow tempo** (**Chowka kala**) and the use of the signature **Guruguha**. He traveled extensively across **India**, incorporating elements of **Hindustani music** into his works.

**Important Points__**

• The five specific **Pancharatna Kritis** are: **Jagadananda Karaka** (Raga Nata), **Dudukugala** (Raga Gaula), **Sadhinchene** (Raga Arabhi), **Kanakanaruchira** (Raga Varali), and **Endaro Mahanubhavulu** (Raga Sri).

• **Jagadananda Karaka** is unique among the five as it is the only one composed entirely in **Sanskrit**, listing **108** names and attributes of **Lord Rama**.

• The **Pancharatna Kritis** are set to **Adi Tala**, which is an **8-beat cycle**. They follow a **Charanam** structure where each stanza is followed by a **Swara-Sahitya** (rhythmic syllables followed by lyrics).

• **Tyagaraja** is said to have composed over **24,000** songs in his lifetime, though only about **700** to **800** are available to us today. His works are characterized by **Bhakti** (devotion) and **Sringara** (beauty).

questions.question: Which of these mountain ranges is not among the ones separating India from the rest of Asia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Arakanyoma**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• The **Indian Subcontinent** is geographically isolated from the rest of the **Asian** continent by a massive barrier of high mountain ranges in the north and northwest.

• The **Himalayas**, **Karakoram**, and **Hindukush** ranges collectively form this physical barrier that separates the **Indian** landmass from **Central Asia** and the **Tibetan Plateau**.

• **Hindukush mountains**: This range extends through **Afghanistan** and **Pakistan**, acting as the northwestern boundary of the subcontinent and separating it from **Central Asia**. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Karakoram mountains**: Situated in the regions of **Ladakh**, **Gilgit-Baltistan**, and **Xinjiang**, this range separates **India** from the **Tarim Basin** and **Central Asian** regions. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Himalayas**: This is the most prominent range that forms the northern boundary of **India**, separating the subcontinent from the **Tibetan Plateau** and the rest of the **Asian** continent. ***Hence, this range is among those separating India from the rest of Asia.***

• **Arakanyoma**: Also known as the **Rakhine Mountains**, this range is located in **Myanmar** and separates the **Irrawaddy** basin from the **Bay of Bengal**. While it forms a boundary between **India** and **Myanmar** in the east, it is not considered part of the primary northern mountain wall that separates the subcontinent from the rest of the **Asian** landmass. ***Hence, this range is not among the ones separating India from the rest of Asia.***

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Himalayas**: These are the youngest fold mountains in the world, formed approximately **50 million years** ago. They stretch for about **2,400 kilometers** from the **Indus River** in the west to the **Brahmaputra River** in the east, containing the world's highest peak, **Mount Everest**, at **8,848.86 meters**.

• **Karakoram Range**: This range contains the highest concentration of glaciers outside the polar regions, including the **Siachen Glacier**. It is home to **K2** (Mount Godwin-Austen), which is the second-highest peak in the world at **8,611 meters**.

• **Hindukush**: Stretching for about **800 kilometers**, this range is historically significant for the **Khyber Pass**, which served as a major trade and invasion route into the **Indian Subcontinent**. Its highest peak is **Tirich Mir**, located in **Pakistan**.

• **Arakanyoma**: This range is a southward extension of the **Himalayas** that arcs through **Myanmar**. It includes the **Patkai**, **Naga**, and **Lushai** hills on the **Indian** side. The highest point of this range is **Mount Victoria** (also known as **Nat Ma Taung**).

**Important Points__**

• **Climatic Barrier**: These northern mountain ranges protect the **Indian Subcontinent** from the freezing cold **Siberian** winds during winter and trap the moisture-laden **Southwest Monsoon** winds, ensuring heavy rainfall in the **Indo-Gangetic Plain**.

• **Biodiversity Hotspots**: The **Himalayas** and the **Indo-Burma** region (which includes the **Arakanyoma**) are recognized as global **Biodiversity Hotspots** due to their unique flora and fauna.

• **River Systems**: Major perennial rivers such as the **Indus**, **Ganges**, and **Brahmaputra** originate from these high mountain ranges, providing a vital source of water for agriculture and life in **India**.
</ul

• Her case remains a landmark in the discussion of **human rights** and **gender ethics** in international sports, alongside athletes like **Caster Semenya**. It highlighted the psychological trauma caused by **sex verification** policies implemented by bodies like **World Athletics** (formerly **IAAF**).

**Important Points__**

• **Gender verification** tests were once mandatory at major sporting events but were largely abolished in the late **1990s**, only to be reintroduced on a case-by-case basis if an athlete's eligibility was questioned.

• The **2006 Doha Asian Games** saw **India** finish with a total of **53 medals**, including **10 gold**, **17 silver**, and **26 bronze**, excluding the stripped medal of **Santhi Soundarajan**.

• Current regulations by **World Athletics** focus on **testosterone** levels in female athletes with **Differences of Sexual Development (DSD)**, requiring them to medically reduce their levels to compete in certain track events.

questions.question: How many countries are there in South Asia?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**8**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• South Asia is a distinct geographical and ethno-cultural region of the world that consists of **8 countries**. These nations are **Afghanistan**, **Bangladesh**, **Bhutan**, **India**, **Maldives**, **Nepal**, **Pakistan**, and **Sri Lanka**.

• The definition of South Asia is often synonymous with the member states of the **South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC)**. While the region originally consisted of **7 founding members**, the number increased to **8** when **Afghanistan** joined the organization.

• **Afghanistan** was formally inducted as the **8th member** of the South Asian group during the **14th SAARC Summit** held in **New Delhi, India**, in **April 2007**. This inclusion expanded the geopolitical definition of the region further into Central Asia.

• Geographically, the region is often referred to as the **Indian Subcontinent**. It is naturally bounded by the **Himalayas** to the north, the **Hindu Kush** to the northwest, and the **Indian Ocean**, **Arabian Sea**, and **Bay of Bengal** to the south, west, and east respectively.

• The region covers an area of approximately **5.2 million square kilometers**, which represents about **11.71% of the Asian continent** and **3.5% of the worlds total land surface**.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **SAARC (South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation)**: This is the primary intergovernmental organization for the region, established on **December 8, 1985**. Its **Secretariat** is based in **Kathmandu, Nepal**, and it serves as a platform for regional integration and economic development.

• **Demographics**: South Asia is the most populous and most densely populated geographical region in the world. It is home to nearly **2 billion people**, which is roughly **one-fourth of the global population**.

• **Economic Diversity**: **India** is the largest economy in the region, contributing significantly to the regional **GDP**. The region is characterized by a mix of developing economies with high growth potential, particularly in sectors like **Information Technology**, **Agriculture**, and **Textiles**.

• **Geographical Classification**: Among the **8 countries**, **Nepal**, **Bhutan**, and **Afghanistan** are **landlocked nations**, meaning they have no direct access to the sea. Conversely, **Sri Lanka** and **Maldives** are **island nations** located in the **Indian Ocean**.

• **Political History**: Most countries in the region share a common history of colonial rule, particularly under the **British Empire**, which has influenced their modern **legal systems**, **administrative structures**, and the widespread use of the **English language**.

**Important Points__**

• **SAFTA (South Asian Free Trade Area)**: An agreement reached in **2004** during the **12th SAARC Summit** in **Islamabad**, aimed at creating a free trade area in the region to boost intra-regional trade among the **8 member nations**.

• **Cultural Heritage**: South Asia is the cradle of several major world religions, including **Hinduism**, **Buddhism**, **Sikhism**, and **Jainism**. It also hosts one of the largest **Muslim** populations in the world across **Pakistan**, **Bangladesh**, and **India**.

• **Environmental Challenges**: The region is highly vulnerable to **climate change**. For instance, **Maldives** faces the threat of rising sea levels, while **Bangladesh** is prone to frequent flooding, and the **Himalayan nations** face risks from melting glaciers.

• **Observer Status**: Apart from the **8 member countries**, several nations and organizations hold **observer status** in SAARC, including **China**, the **European Union**, **Japan**, **South Korea**, and the **United States**.
</ul

questions.question: What does HDI stand for?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Human Development Index**__.

**__Key Points__**
__

• **HDI** stands for **Human Development Index**, which is a statistical composite index used to measure the average achievements of a country in three basic dimensions of human development. ***Hence, the correct answer is Human Development Index.***

• The concept of the **Human Development Index** was created by the Pakistani economist **Mahbub ul Haq** and the Indian economist **Amartya Sen** in **1990**.

• It is published annually by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)** as part of the **Human Development Report (HDR)**.

• The index was designed to shift the focus of development economics from national income accounting to people-centered policies, emphasizing that people and their capabilities should be the ultimate criteria for assessing the development of a country.

• It ranks countries into four levels of human development: **Very High**, **High**, **Medium**, and **Low** based on their cumulative score across various indicators.

**Additional Information__**
__

• **Health Dimension**: This is assessed by **Life Expectancy at birth**, which is the average number of years a person is expected to live based on current mortality rates. It serves as a proxy for the overall health and nutrition status of a population.

• **Education Dimension**: This is calculated using two indicators: **Mean years of schooling** (the average number of years of education received by people ages **25** and older) and **Expected years of schooling** (the total number of years of schooling that a child of school-entry age can expect to receive).

• **Standard of Living**: This is assessed by **Gross National Income (GNI) per capita** at **Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)** in international **US Dollars**. This measure accounts for the differences in the cost of living and inflation between countries.

• The **HDI** score is a value between **0 and 1**. A score closer to **1** indicates a higher level of development, while a score closer to **0** indicates a lower level.

• The **UNDP** uses the **geometric mean** of the three normalized dimension indices to calculate the final **HDI** value, ensuring that a low achievement in one dimension is not linearly compensated by a high achievement in another.

**Important Points__**

• In the latest **Human Development Report 2023-24**, **India** was ranked **134th** out of **193 countries** with an **HDI** value of **0.644**, placing it in the **Medium** human development category.

• **Switzerland**, **Norway**, and **Iceland** consistently rank at the top of the global **Human Development Index** due to their high life expectancy and robust social security systems.

• The **UNDP** also tracks other vital indices like the **Gender Inequality Index (GII)**, where **India** ranked **108th** in the **2022** report, showing improvement in gender parity.

• The **Inequality-adjusted Human Development Index (IHDI)** accounts for the distribution of achievements within a population; the difference between the **HDI** and **IHDI** represents the loss in human development due to inequality.

• The **Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)** complements the **HDI** by identifying overlapping deprivations at the household and individual level in health, education, and living standards, providing a more comprehensive view of poverty than income alone.
</ul

The correct answer is __**Sarojini Naidu**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **National Women's Day** in India is celebrated every year on **February 13** to commemorate the birth anniversary of **Sarojini Naidu**, a pivotal figure in India's independence movement.
 
• Born on **February 13, 1879**, in **Hyderabad**, she was a renowned poet and is widely known by the sobriquet **"Nightingale of India"** or **"Bharat Kokila"** due to the lyrical and melodic quality of her poetry.
 
• She made history in **1925** when she was elected as the **first Indian woman President** of the **Indian National Congress** at the **Kanpur Session**.
 
• Following India's independence in **1947**, she was appointed as the **Governor of the United Provinces** (now known as **Uttar Pradesh**), making her the **first woman to hold the office of Governor** in independent India.

questions.question: What is the major reason for the shrinking of the Himalayan glaciers?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Global warming**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Global warming** is identified as the primary driver behind the rapid **shrinking and retreat** of **Himalayan glaciers**. This phenomenon refers to the long-term increase in the **average surface temperature** of the Earth due to human activities. ***Hence, the statement is correct.***
 
• The **Himalayas**, known as the **Third Pole**, hold the largest concentration of **frozen water** outside the North and South Poles. These glaciers are highly sensitive to **climatic fluctuations**.
 
• The primary mechanism of shrinking involves the **negative mass balance** of glaciers, where the rate of **ablation** (melting and evaporation) exceeds the rate of **accumulation** (snowfall) due to rising atmospheric temperatures.
 
• The accumulation of **Greenhouse Gases (GHGs)** such as **Carbon Dioxide (CO2)**, **Methane (CH4)**, and **Nitrous Oxide (N2O)** traps solar radiation within the Earth's atmosphere, creating a warming effect that accelerates the melting of **alpine glaciers**.
 
• According to various scientific assessments, the **Himalayan region** is warming at a rate higher than the **global average**, leading to the formation of **supraglacial lakes** and increased risks of **Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs)**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Black Carbon:** Apart from general global warming, the deposition of **Black Carbon** (soot) on glacier surfaces significantly contributes to melting. Produced by the **incomplete combustion** of fossil fuels and biomass, these dark particles reduce the **albedo effect** (reflectivity) of snow, causing it to absorb more **solar energy**.
 
• **ICIMOD Reports:** The **International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD)** released a landmark report stating that even if global warming is capped at **1.5 degrees Celsius**, at least **one-third** of the Himalayan glaciers will vanish by the year **2100**.
 
• **River Systems:** The shrinking of these glaciers directly impacts perennial river systems like the **Ganga**, **Indus**, and **Brahmaputra**. These rivers provide water security to nearly **1.9 billion people** across **India**, **China**, **Pakistan**, **Nepal**, and **Bhutan**.
 
• **The Gangotri Glacier:** Located in the **Uttarkashi district** of **Uttarakhand**, it is one of the largest glaciers in the Himalayas. It has been retreating at a rate of approximately **10 to 30 meters per year** over the last few decades.
 
• **Impact on Ecosystems:** The loss of glacial volume alters the **hydrological cycle**, leading to unpredictable **seasonal water flow**, which adversely affects **agriculture**, **hydroelectric power generation**, and **biodiversity** in the **Hindu Kush Himalayan (HKH)** region.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Paris Agreement (2015):** An international treaty aimed at limiting **global warming** to well below **2 degrees Celsius** above pre-industrial levels is crucial for the preservation of the **cryosphere**.
 
• **Satellite Monitoring:** Agencies like **ISRO** (Indian Space Research Organisation) and **NASA** use **Remote Sensing** and **GIS** technology to monitor the health of **over 9,000 glaciers** in the Indian Himalayan region.
 
• **Albedo Feedback:** As white ice melts, it exposes darker land or water underneath, which absorbs more heat, leading to a **self-reinforcing cycle** of further warming and melting.
 
• **Holocene Epoch:** While glaciers have advanced and retreated naturally over **geological time scales**, the current rate of retreat is unprecedented and primarily **anthropogenic** (human-induced).
